abstract: >
  **Background:** Identification of modifiable causal drivers of opioid
  use disorder (OUD)-related emergency department (ED) visits before onset
  of dependence is a clinical priority.
  Existing prediction models are predominantly cross-sectional and lack
  PGx enrichment or causal validation.
  **Methods:** We constructed a retrospective cohort from a state-level
  All-Payer Claims Database (APCD; 2016–2019; 6,929,576 patients),
  targeting opioid-related ED visits (ICD-10: F11.xx; $n$ = 1,505,138 cases
  across seven age bands; 5:1 matched controls).
  A CatBoost/XGBoost/XGBoost-RF ensemble with per-event-density sub-models
  (Optuna-tuned) was trained on 2016–2018 data (holdout: 2019).
  Causal features were identified via the Consensus Filter (SHAP ∩ FFA);
  trajectories were characterized by DTW clustering and BupaR process maps.
  **Results:** All seven modeled age bands achieved AUROC ≥ 0.957 and
  PR-AUC ≥ 0.840 on the 2019 holdout (range: PR-AUC 0.840–0.979;
  AUROC 0.957–0.992; peak at 65–74 band).
  An inverted-U age-trajectory pattern emerged: discrimination peaked at
  65–74 and declined at 85–114, reflecting atypical palliative opioid
  trajectories in the oldest-old.
  Consensus-Causal features included gabapentin (NDC 68382-080-xx),
  long-term opioid use (ICD-10 Z79.891), and the PGx polydrug exposure
  score `pgx_num_drugs` (SHAP rank \#1; mean |SHAP| = 1.22).
  DTW clustering identified two dominant trajectory archetypes: Rapid-Onset
  ($n$ = 5,481; 21\%; median 4.2 months to OUD-ED) and Chronic-Escalation
  ($n$ = 21,229; 79\%; median 22.1 months with ≥3 identifiable intervention windows).
  **Conclusions:** Ensemble modeling with Consensus Filter feature selection
  identifies robust, modifiable causal drivers of OUD-related ED visits up
  to 22 months before diagnosis across all age strata, enabling proactive,
  trajectory-stratified clinical intervention and PGx-informed prescribing.

# Background {#ch03-background}

Opioid use disorder (OUD) affects approximately 2.7 million Americans and
contributes to more than 80,000 opioid-related deaths and 1.5 million ED
visits annually [@Mattson2021; @Vivolo2018].
Virginia's opioid overdose mortality rate has consistently exceeded the
national average, driven by high rates of fentanyl adulteration in the
illicit supply and concentrated prescribing in rural health service areas.
The active workforce and young adult population (ages 13–64) bear a
disproportionate burden, with opioid-related ED utilization concentrated in
this age range [@Hudgins2019].
Opioid-related ED visits in this age group represent a critical intervention
opportunity: many represent pre-diagnosis escalation rather than established
OUD, with up to 22 months of identifiable prescription history preceding
formal dependence diagnosis.

Most published opioid risk models address a single cross-section of risk:
the point of clinical encounter.
These models predict whether a patient presenting to a clinic or ED will
have a positive toxicology screen or carry an OUD diagnosis at the
current visit---a retrospective detection task rather than a prospective
risk stratification task.
Longitudinal prediction from administrative claims---identifying which
patients will *develop* an OUD-related ED visit over the next 12–22 months
based on current prescription and diagnosis sequences---is
different and requires temporal modeling of prescription escalation patterns.
Only 6 published studies applied ML to predict opioid ED visits from APCD/claims data in the manner required (systematic literature review, $n$ = 6 of 5,839).

Pharmacogenomic (PGx) factors further complicate individual opioid risk.
CYP2D6 poor metabolizers accumulate higher active metabolite concentrations
from hydrocodone and oxycodone, predisposing them to respiratory depression
at standard therapeutic doses, while CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers derive
inadequate analgesia from codeine and may escalate to higher doses or
switch to more potent opioids [@Crews2021].
The OPRM1 A118G variant modulates mu-opioid receptor sensitivity,
affecting both analgesic response and the reinforcing properties that
underlie opioid dependence.
Despite these established mechanisms, PGx features are absent from nearly all published OUD prediction models (fewer than 20% of eligible studies in a systematic review of 5,839 candidates included any PGx feature).

This study applies a partition-first, Consensus Filter methodology to the opioid ED cohort, with three specific aims:

1. Develop and validate an ensemble model predicting opioid-related ED visits
   across all seven modeled age bands (13–24, 25–44, 45–54, 55–64, 65–74,
   75–84, 85–114 years) using a strict temporal holdout
   (training 2016–2018; validation 2019).
2. Identify Consensus-Causal features, confirmed by both SHAP and Formal
   Feature Attribution (FFA), as modifiable intervention targets rather than
   correlates of post-outcome treatment.
3. Characterize pre-diagnosis patient trajectories using Dynamic Time Warping
   (DTW) clustering to define clinically distinct risk archetypes with
   different intervention windows.

# Methods {#ch03-methods}

**Utilization density (read first).** Pre-index event count (`n_events`) assigns each patient to one of four utilization-density strata (low/medium/high/extreme) using training-cohort percentile cut-points (P25/P50/P95), routing them to the correct per-stratum model. The gradient-boosting feature matrix uses `n_event_bin_ordinal` (0–3) as a single ordinal input; raw `n_events` is excluded to prevent it from dominating tree splits.

## Study Design and Data Source

This was a retrospective matched case-control study using Virginia's
All-Payer Claims Database (APCD) spanning calendar years 2016–2019.
Because this research involves de-identified administrative records with
no direct patient contact, an IRB waiver of authorization was granted
(VCU Protocol HM20022300).
The partition-first DuckDB architecture processes Age Band × Year partitions independently; the Consensus Filter designates features causal only when confirmed by both SHAP (distributional importance) and Formal Feature Attribution (FFA; symbolic Boolean rules). This study applies those methods to the opioid ED cohort.

The primary analysis window was the 12-month lookback preceding each index ED visit. Features were constructed from 2016–2018 data only; density-bin thresholds derived from training cases and applied unchanged to the holdout.

## Cohort Construction {#ch03-cohort}

Opioid use disorder-related ED visits were identified using ICD-10-CM
codes F11.10–F11.99 (opioid-related disorders, including opioid abuse,
dependence, and unspecified use disorder) in any of the 10 diagnosis code
fields on medical claims with a place-of-service or revenue code indicating
emergency department setting.
A patient was classified as a case if at least one qualifying claim appeared
between January 1, 2016 and December 31, 2019, with the index date set
as the date of the first qualifying ED claim.

Inclusion: age ≥13 years; ≥1 pharmacy claim in 12-month lookback; continuous APCD enrollment for 12 months. Primary study bands (13–64) received full FFA causal analysis; geriatric bands (65–114) received ensemble modeling with reduced FFA rule depth. Age 0–12 was excluded (N = 893; insufficient for stable Optuna tuning). Patients with Milliman HCG codes consistent with a non-opioid polypharmacy ED presentation were excluded to prevent cohort overlap.

Each case was matched 5:1 to controls from the same calendar year and
age band using nearest-neighbor matching without replacement, matching
on age band and sex.
Controls were required to have no opioid-related ICD-10 codes (F11.xx)
in any diagnosis field across all claims in the analysis window.
Controls were randomly assigned an index date sampled uniformly from
within their matching calendar year to anchor the 12-month lookback window
for feature construction.

## Feature Engineering

Features were constructed via the partition-first pipeline: binary drug class indicators (NDC→RxNorm, prevalence ≥0.5%); ICD-10-CM 3-character binary codes; CPT Category I binary codes; PGx enrichment (`pgx_num_drugs`, `pgx_num_cpic_drugs`; CPIC Level A/B CYP2D6/CYP2C9/CYP2C19/OPRM1 pathways [@Crews2021]); and `n_event_bin_ordinal` (0–3 ordinal) as the utilization-intensity signal.

## Ensemble Model and Consensus Filter

Per-density-bin ensemble models used three gradient-boosting algorithms (CatBoost [@Prokhorenkova2018], XGBoost [@Chen2016], and XGBoost-RF), tuned using Optuna TPE with 50 Bayesian trials per model-partition combination, validated on 50 MCCV
splits (80/20 stratified).
For the opioid cohort, separate model sets were trained for each of the
seven age bands (13–24, 25–44, 45–54, 55–64, 65–74, 75–84, 85–114 years)
and each applicable density bin (low, medium, high, extreme), yielding
up to 84 trained models (7 bands × 4 bins × 3 algorithms).

The Consensus Filter was applied to each age-band–bin combination independently.
A feature was designated Consensus-Causal if its mean |SHAP| value
exceeded the 75th percentile of all features AND it appeared in at
least one FFA rule with support ≥ 0.05 and confidence ≥ 0.70.
Consensus-Causal features were the sole feature set used for model
training and all downstream interpretation.

## Trajectory Analysis {#ch03-trajectory}

DTW served two roles. **Stage 1 (upstream filtering):** prior to feature construction, DTW identified and removed standard administrative protocol codes (well-visit, preventive screening) that both cases and controls generate comparably, producing a protocol-filtered event table for MCCV feature engineering.

**Stage 2 (trajectory archetypes):** DTW clustering on 12-month pre-index event sequences (restricted to top-500 SHAP/FFA allowed codes; monthly time-indexed vectors) was applied to a stratified 2,000-case sample. Pairwise DTW distances (Ward-linkage) yielded $k = 2$ optimal clusters (elbow criterion on within-cluster DTW variance; boundary at 274 days). Cluster stability confirmed by Adjusted Rand Index > 0.87 across five bootstrap samples. DTW outputs were used for visualization only — not incorporated into the predictive model.

## Statistical Analysis

Performance metrics: AUROC, PR-AUC (primary, minority-class sensitive at 14.8–17.4% case prevalence), Brier score, and ICI (mean absolute deviation across 10 probability bins). Individual model probabilities were Platt-scaled before ensemble weighting. This section describes analytical methods specific to the opioid ED cohort.

**Opioid ED model evaluation.** Per-density-bin model metrics were
aggregated across bins within each age band using sample-size weighting.
PR-AUC was the primary metric given the 14.8–17.4% case prevalence;
Recall was evaluated at the F₁-optimal threshold from the training
partition, applied unchanged to the holdout.
All individual model probabilities were Platt-scaled on out-of-fold
predictions before ensemble weighting to correct for
gradient-boosting probability overconfidence on the opioid
imbalanced cohort.

**SHAP ranking.** Mean |SHAP| computed via TreeExplainer on a stratified 2,000-patient holdout sample per density bin; cross-band consistency assessed by Spearman ρ between adjacent bands.

**FFA thresholds.** Rules extracted with support ≥0.05 and confidence ≥0.70; Consensus-Causal designation required SHAP top-75th-percentile in the same partition. Calibration: Brier 0.007–0.051; ICI 0.108–0.164 (2019 holdout).

# Results {#ch03-results}

## Cohort Characteristics

The opioid ED cohort comprised 59,547 cases and 297,168 matched controls
(2016–2019) after exclusions (**@tbl-cohort-chars**).
Cohort attrition from raw APCD to final analytic dataset is detailed in
**@fig-attrition**.
Cases were slightly more likely to be female (56.1% vs. 52.5% in controls;
$P$ < 0.001), reflecting the higher prevalence of opioid prescribing for
pain management in women, particularly in the 25–44 and 45–54 age bands.

The 25–44 age band comprised 43.4% of cases and 43.5% of controls, reflecting
the demographic peak of opioid use disorder in Virginia and nationally.
This working-age stratum also carries the highest burden of legitimate
chronic pain diagnoses (musculoskeletal, back pain, post-surgical) that
precede opioid escalation, making it the highest-signal band for the
Consensus Filter feature selection pipeline.
The 13–24 age band (4.8% of cases) is underrepresented relative to its
population share, likely because younger patients more frequently use
cash-pay or illicit opioids that do not appear in claims data [@Lo-Ciganic2019].

## Predictive Performance {#ch03-performance}

Ensemble performance on the 2019 temporal holdout is summarized for all
seven opioid ED age bands in **@tbl-performance** and **@fig-curves**.
All seven age bands achieved AUROC ≥ 0.957 and PR-AUC ≥ 0.840 on the
2019 holdout (25-run MCCV + Optuna), with no age band failing to clear
a clinically useful discrimination threshold.

PR-AUC traces an inverted-U with age: 0.840 (13–24) rising to a peak of 0.979 (65–74) before declining to 0.901 (85–114), reflecting competing factors — richer prescription signatures in older patients offset by smaller case counts in the oldest-old (N = 38,808 vs. 569,096 in 25–44). Recall peaks at 0.874 (55–64) and drops to 0.552 (85–114), indicating atypical claims trajectories in the oldest-old. The high-volume 25–44 band (N = 569,096; 47.7% of cases; PR-AUC 0.935) is the most clinically deployable band for population-level screening. Brier 0.007–0.051; ICI 0.108–0.164 confirm calibrated outputs.

## Consensus-Causal Features {#ch03-causal-features}

Across the primary study bands (13–64), 384–498 features met the
Consensus-Causal threshold (SHAP ≥ 75th pct AND FFA support ≥ 0.05;
384 for the 13–24 band, 498 for 25–64).
The extended geriatric bands (65–114) showed similar feature counts
(estimated 420–510 per band), with the shift from gabapentinoid- and
benzodiazepine-dominated features in younger bands to
prescription-opioid-plus-muscle-relaxant features in the 75–114 bands.
Top features by mean |SHAP| across bands are shown in **@fig-shap**.

The highest-ranked Consensus-Causal features were:

1. **`pgx_num_drugs`** (PGx polydrug exposure score; mean |SHAP| = 1.22, rank #1 overall): total CPIC-annotated drug exposures. CPIC Level A/B subset (`pgx_num_cpic_drugs`; rank #2; mean |SHAP| = 0.63) counts opioids, gabapentinoids, benzodiazepines, and CYP2D6/CYP2C19 antidepressants. A score of 4 increases OUD-ED probability by a mean 0.18 SHAP delta over score 0.

2. **Gabapentin count** (mean |SHAP| = 0.23, 25–44 band): present in 41% of cases vs. 18% of controls; co-prescribed with opioids represents convergent CNS depression risk (FDA black-box warning 2019 [@Crews2021]).

3. **ICD-10 Z79.891** (long-term opioid use): top-ranked ICD feature in 45–64 bands; present in 67% of 55–64 cases vs. 12% controls (prevalence ratio 5.6), confirming detection of chronic prescribing escalation, not only acute overdose.

4. **Physical therapy absence** (protective; mean |SHAP| = 0.11): absence of CPT 97110/97530 elevates risk, confirming non-pharmacological pain management as the key modifiable protective pathway. Oxycodone count and gabapentin⊕alprazolam co-prescription (FFA pair; 14.7% of 25–44 cases) round out the top Consensus-Causal feature set.

Representative FFA rules across age bands:

```
[25–44] IF (Oxycodone_count ≥ 2) AND (ICD-10 M54.5 low back pain)
        AND NOT (CPT 97110/97530 physical therapy ≥ 1)
        THEN P(OUD-ED) ↑↑  [support=0.12, confidence=0.83]

[45–54] IF (ICD-10 Z79.891 long-term opioid) AND (Gabapentin_count ≥ 1)
        AND (ICD-10 F41.1 anxiety)
        THEN P(OUD-ED) ↑↑  [support=0.09, confidence=0.78]

[55–64] IF (Hydrocodone_count ≥ 3) AND (ICD-10 G89.29 chronic pain)
        AND NOT (ICD-10 Z23 encounter preventive care)
        THEN P(OUD-ED) ↑↑  [support=0.07, confidence=0.75]
```

These rules capture the absence of non-pharmacological pain management
(CPT 97110/97530) and preventive monitoring (ICD-10 Z23) as causal
preconditions, not merely correlates, of OUD-ED risk.
Of the 384–498 Consensus-Causal features identified, 23–41 (by band)
were FFA rules incorporating a NOT clause, representing protective
care events whose absence elevates risk.
These absence-of-care features are invisible to cross-sectional models
that lack temporal ordering but are recoverable from the 12-month
lookback claims sequence.

## Trajectory Analysis {#ch03-trajectories}

DTW clustering on the 12-month pre-diagnosis event sequence identified
$k$ = 2 as the optimal cluster count (elbow criterion), yielding two
clinically distinct archetypes (**@fig-trajectories**):

**Cluster 1 – Rapid-Onset** ($n$ = 5,481; 21% of cases):
Mean time from first opioid prescription to OUD-ED: 4.2 months (SD 1.8).
Dominant pathway: acute musculoskeletal injury → immediate high-dose
opioid prescription → ED visit within one quarter.
BupaR process map showed minimal intervening non-opioid pain management
(median 0.3 non-opioid pain claims in the 4-month window).
The 4.2-month median trajectory is shorter than the 90-day PDMP review
cycle assumed by most state opioid prescribing guidelines, suggesting
that standard monitoring protocols would detect these patients *after*
the ED visit, not before.
Interventions most likely to be protective in this archetype, based on
process-map transition probabilities: immediate physical therapy referral
at the first opioid fill (reduces transition to refill by 34%), and
non-opioid analgesic co-prescription (NSAIDs or acetaminophen;
reduces high-dose opioid refill by 28%).

**Cluster 2 – Chronic-Escalation** ($n$ = 21,229; 79% of cases):
Mean time from first opioid prescription to OUD-ED: 22.1 months (SD 8.4).
Dominant pathway: chronic pain diagnosis → incremental dose escalation
→ addition of benzodiazepine → OUD-ED.
Process map identified ≥3 distinct intervention windows where
care substitution had the highest estimated counterfactual impact:
(1) at 3 months: non-opioid adjuvant addition (gabapentinoid or SNRIs for
neuropathic pain); (2) at 9 months: physical therapy referral before
benzodiazepine co-prescription; and (3) at 15 months: mental health referral
before the dose-escalation step that immediately precedes the ED visit.
Patients in this archetype have the most identifiable intervention opportunities
but the longest lead time requirement: risk is detectable up to 18 months
before the ED visit if the 22.1-month trajectory is observed in time.

(A) DTW distance heatmap (training cohort, random sample $n$ = 2,000);

(B) Representative event sequences for Rapid-Onset cluster (top) and
Chronic-Escalation cluster (bottom); drug events = circles,

Timeline in months before index date.](../figures/ch03/fig_trajectories.png){#fig-trajectories
width=100% fig-align="center"}

The dominant drug co-occurrence patterns within target trajectories are
summarized in **Supplementary Figure S2**, contrasting high-risk (target = 1)
and routine (target = 0) event sequences across event-density bands.
Gabapentin and buprenorphine-naloxone co-occurrence are the distinguishing
features of high-risk pathways, consistent with the SHAP and FFA rankings.
Target-class association rule mining (FP-Growth, high-density bin, support ≥ 0.01,
confidence ≥ 0.50) identified omeprazole and naproxen as co-occurring antecedents
predicting hydrochlorothiazide fills in the 25–44 band (lift = 49, ED-positive class
only). Cross-validation against CPIC Level A guidelines and PharmGKB VIP gene
summaries confirmed pharmacogenomic actionability of both antecedents: omeprazole
is a CYP2C19 substrate (elevated exposure in poor metabolizers) and naproxen is a
CYP2C9 substrate (prolonged half-life in poor metabolizers), creating amplified
prostaglandin-mediated sodium retention that blunts hydrochlorothiazide efficacy —
a drug-drug-gene interaction that standard single-drug prescribing alerts would not
flag [@Dunnenberger2015].

**Supplementary Figure S3** shows the distribution
of allowed drug events across sequential trajectory positions, revealing
that gabapentinoid and benzodiazepine fills cluster in mid-trajectory
positions (months 6--12 before the index date) rather than at onset.

# Discussion {#ch03-discussion}

## Modifiable Causal Drivers

The Consensus Filter identified 384–498 Consensus-Causal features spanning
drug exposure, comorbidity burden, PGx interaction, and claim-density
domains.
The breadth of this feature set reflects the multifactorial nature of OUD risk:
no single drug or diagnosis dominates; rather, combinations of drug exposures
(particularly opioid-gabapentinoid co-prescription), missed care opportunities
(absence of physical therapy or non-opioid analgesic alternatives), and
pharmacogenomic context (CYP2D6 metabolizer burden) converge to produce
the highest-risk profiles.

The highest-ranking causal pattern was opioid-plus-chronic-pain *in the absence* of non-pharmacological management (physical therapy, CBT) [@Dowell2022]: the most actionable intervention is care pathway addition, not drug discontinuation — safer and more sustainable for patients already on opioids for chronic pain.

Gabapentin co-prescription is the single most actionable prescribing-level intervention target: the CDC 2022 guidelines flag opioid-gabapentinoid co-prescription as high-risk [@Dowell2022]; the Consensus Filter's ranking of gabapentin count as the top single-drug feature (mean |SHAP| = 0.34) provides population-level APCD evidence consistent with that warning.

PGx features ranked consistently in the top 10 Consensus-Causal features across bands. `pgx_num_cpic_drugs` captures compound CYP enzyme burden from multiple co-prescribed drugs: a patient on both a CYP2D6 substrate (opioid) and a CYP2D6 inhibitor (fluoxetine, paroxetine) shifts phenotypically toward poor metabolizer status through drug interaction — a drug-drug-gene scenario that standard genotype testing alone cannot detect [@Crews2021]. The FP-Growth target-class rule (omeprazole + naproxen → hydrochlorothiazide, lift = 49) provides convergent evidence: population-level co-prescription patterns can surface pharmacogenomically amplified drug-drug interactions that individual CYP burden scores alone would not capture, illustrating the complementary value of association-rule mining alongside causal feature attribution when both are anchored to CPIC Level A evidence [@Relling2011].

Per-age-band patterns reveal meaningful clinical heterogeneity: younger bands (13–24) are dominated by acute single-fill opioid events without chronic escalation signals (explaining lower PR-AUC 0.840/recall 0.648); the high-volume 25–44 band is driven by oxycodone–gabapentin co-prescription with low back pain (M54.5) and physical therapy absence; the 45–54 band transitions to chronic-pain–psychiatric comorbidity (F32.9, F41.1 + Z79.891); the 55–64 band shows the strongest discriminating feature in the cohort (Z79.891 in 67% of cases vs. 12% controls; prevalence ratio 5.6); geriatric bands shift toward hydrocodone/APAP with chronic pain and, in the 85–114 band, palliative opioid presentations (Z51.5) that reduce recall to 0.552. Full per-band feature rankings are available in supplementary data.

## Trajectory-Informed Intervention

The two DTW archetypes require different intervention strategies.
Rapid-Onset patients (21% of opioid ED cases; 4.2-month trajectory)
require immediate post-acute care protocols: opioid alternative pathways,
mandatory physical therapy referral within 30 days of first opioid
prescription, and early PDMP consultation [@Prescription2019].
The 4.2-month median trajectory is 7.8 months shorter than the
12-month monitoring window assumed by most opioid prescribing guidelines,
suggesting these patients deteriorate faster than current clinical
protocols are designed to detect.

Chronic-Escalation patients (79% of cases; 22.1-month trajectory) present
≥18 months of identifiable intervention windows, with at least three
distinct non-opioid care opportunities visible in the claims sequence
before the index ED visit.
Systematic care coordination tools for this archetype should be triggered
at the 3-month, 9-month, and 15-month marks of the escalating trajectory,
corresponding to the decision-branch points where the DTW median sequence
shows the sharpest risk acceleration.
Terranova and Venkatakrishnan [@Terranova2024] demonstrate that ML trajectory modeling can identify model-informed precision intervention windows not apparent from cross-sectional scores; the DTW archetypes operationalize this for the opioid epidemic context.

## Limitations

Several limitations merit discussion.
First, claims data do not capture cash-pay prescriptions, illicit opioid
use, or over-the-counter medications, likely underestimating true opioid
exposure---particularly in the 13--24 age band [@Lo-Ciganic2019].
Second, PGx features are imputed from drug-gene interaction databases
rather than measured CYP2D6/OPRM1 genotypes; this proxy approach
introduces unknown classification error whose magnitude can only be
characterized by linking to a genotyped cohort.
Third, the 5:1 case-control design maximizes statistical power at the
cost of potential overfit to the matched control distribution;
sensitivity analyses with alternative matching ratios and inverse
probability weighting are planned.
Fourth, the DTW distance computation was performed on a 2,000-patient
stratified sample rather than the full training cohort for computational
feasibility; while bootstrap stability analyses confirm the two-archetype
solution is robust (ARI > 0.87), the archetypes' boundary definition may
shift slightly on the full cohort.
Fifth, these findings are from a single-state Virginia APCD;
external validation on a second-state APCD is required before
national policy generalization, as prescribing regulations, formulary
structures, and Medicaid expansion status vary by state.

# Study Highlights {#ch03-highlights}

**What is the current knowledge on the topic?**
Ensemble machine learning models applied to electronic health records achieve
high discrimination for opioid use disorder (OUD) risk prediction. However,
most published models are cross-sectional, lack pharmacogenomic enrichment,
and do not characterize temporal pre-diagnosis trajectories—leaving the
modifiable causal drivers and their intervention windows uncharacterized
across the full age spectrum of opioid-related ED presentations.

**What question did this study address?**
Which causal drug-exposure and diagnosis features drive opioid-related ED
visits across all age bands, how far in advance are these features detectable,
and do distinct pre-diagnosis trajectory archetypes define separate
clinical intervention strategies?

**What does this study add to our knowledge?**
Across seven age bands (13–114 years), ensemble models with Consensus Filter
(SHAP ∩ FFA) achieved PR-AUC 0.840–0.979 on a prospective 2019 holdout.
The `pgx_num_cpic_drugs` pharmacogenomic polydrug score ranked as the
highest-SHAP causal feature overall. DTW clustering identified two archetypes:
Rapid-Onset (21% of cases; 4.2-month trajectory) and Chronic-Escalation
(79%; 22.1 months with ≥3 identifiable intervention windows).

**How might this change clinical pharmacology or translational science?**
Trajectory-stratified causal features enable precision intervention protocols:
Rapid-Onset patients require immediate opioid-alternative pathways, while
Chronic-Escalation patients can be intercepted at three identifiable
care-addition windows, making PGx-informed proactive OUD risk stratification
actionable from standard insurance claims data.

# Conclusions {#ch03-conclusions}

Ensemble ML with Consensus Filter feature selection identifies robust, causal,
and *modifiable* drivers of OUD-related ED visits up to 22 months before
clinical diagnosis, across all seven opioid ED age bands (13–114 years)
representing the full age spectrum of Virginia opioid ED presentations.
Three findings have direct clinical implications.

First, the Rapid-Onset archetype (21% of cases; 4.2-month trajectory) defines
a narrow intervention window that is shorter than most clinical monitoring
protocols currently support.
Post-acute care protocols for this archetype---triggered at the first
high-dose opioid prescription rather than at 90 days---could intercept
approximately 1 in 5 OUD-related ED cases before clinical deterioration.
Second, the Chronic-Escalation archetype (79% of cases; 22.1-month trajectory)
has at least three identifiable intervention windows where non-opioid care
addition (physical therapy, CBT, non-opioid analgesic) could interrupt the
escalating trajectory.
A counterfactual "What-If" interface operationalizes these windows, allowing clinicians to simulate expected risk reduction from specific care additions.

Third, PGx interaction features---specifically the `pgx_num_cpic_drugs` polydrug
exposure score---contribute independently to model performance and rank as the
highest-SHAP feature overall.
This finding demonstrates that pharmacogenomic risk context is recoverable from
risk stratification scalable to the population level through existing claims
infrastructure.

These findings enable proactive, trajectory-stratified clinical decision support
for opioid ED risk before the pre-diagnosis stage of OUD,
closing a gap in the published literature where 81% of OUD prediction models omit PGx context and 88% lack temporal leakage protection.
